Deep eutectic solvents boosting solubilization and Se-functionalization of heteropolysaccharide: Multiple hydrogen bonds modulation
Yaxu Sunª, Xiaoyan Jiaª, Ru Yangª, Xiaojie Qinª, Xiaoxue Zhouª, Hui Zhang a, b, c, Weibao Kong a, b, c, Ji Zhang a, b, c, Junlong Wang a, b, c, *

ª College of Life Science, Northwest Normal University, Lanzhou 730070, People's Republic of China b Bioactive Products Engineering Research Center For Gansu Distinctive Plants, Northwest Normal University, Lanzhou 730070, People's Republic of China c Institute of New Rural Development, Northwest Normal University, Lanzhou 730070, People's Republic of China
ARTICLE INFO Keywords: Deep eutectic solvents Hydrogen bond interaction Heteropolysaccharide dissolution Se-functionalization

ABSTRACT In this study, the favorable feasibility of deep eutectic solvents (DESs) in solubilization and functionalization of natural heteropolysaccharide was validated by experiments and density functional theory calculations. This revealed that choline chloride-based DES/DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide) binary mixed solvents possessed more and stronger hydrogen bonding sites, facilitating the balance between disruption and reconstruction of hydrogen bonds within branched heteropolysaccharide from *Artemisia sphaerocephala* (PAS) and achieving efficient solubilization. Further, due to the full exposure and activation of polysaccharide hydroxyls, the efficiency of DES/ DMSO-mediated novel Se-functionalization was substantially enhanced compared to the conventional selenylation methods. The derivative exhibited conversion to lower molecular mass with rigid solution conformation based on co-solvent effect and predominant acidic environment influence. This study offered a framework for exploring the potential of individualized polysaccharide functionalization by modulating DES constituents to achieve multiple controllabilities in terms of conversion efficiency and derivative structure.

# 1. Introduction The ever increasing demands for resources in modern society and the promotion of environmental protection have led to a growing global concern for sustainable natural biological resource (Xu, Che, et al., 2019). In particular, polysaccharide resources of natural biological origin have been used in fuels, materials and pharmaceuticals (Mika et al., 2018). Limitations of structural properties make many natural polysaccharides biologically inactive, hence functionalization strategy becomes an effective way to develop polysaccharide resources (Li et al., 2016). However, owing to the complex structures and the presence of multiple hydrogen bond networks of polysaccharides, organic solvents that mediate polysaccharides functionalization in traditional reaction systems present poor abilities to dissolve polysaccharides and draw-backs such as wastewater contamination and biological toxicity (Farrán et al., 2015). The resulting non-homogeneous environment generally leads to reduced functionalization efficiencies of polysaccharides, which is not conducive to the exploitation of biological resources. Accordingly, the functionalized valorized development of natural resources requires
new solvents and reaction media to achieve the mutual promotion and coordination between the efficient utilization of resources and ecolog- ical environmental protection.

Green solvents are a class of environmentally friendly solvents that have been widely used in the development of biological resources in recent years, among which deep eutectic solvents (DESs) prepared by the hydrogen bond interactions between hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) and hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) are considered to possess great potential for macromolecular biotransformation (Hansen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2012). The hydrogen bond providing/accepting ability of DESs can break hydrogen bonds between carbohydrates, while DESs exhibit high designability, low toxicity and low volatility (Chen & Mu, 2019). At the same time, the high viscosity and thermal decompo- sition exhibited by parts of DESs (González-Rivera et al., 2020; Rodri- guez Rodriguez et al., 2019) make the application of DESs to the processing of natural polysaccharides full of opportunities and chal- lenges. Moreover, the great dissolving performance of DES for poly- saccharide could be enhanced by building binary mixed solvents system to further reduce the viscosity, leading to lower experimental cost and

The dual solvent-solute/solvent interac- tion existing in the mixed solvents can further affect the reaction effi- ciency via solvent effects (Reichardt & Welton, 2011; Ruan et al., 2021). Hereby, much attention has been paid to investigating the interaction between co-solvents and DESs as well as the effect of modulating sol- vents on the functionalization of polysaccharide resources.

Se-functionalization is an important approach to enhance the activity of natural polysaccharides and has been widely reported in recent years as a promising modification of natural polysaccharides (Li et al., 2019; Xu, Wu, et al., 2019). Our previous works achieved selenylation of natural heteropolysaccharide and revealed that in case of modified heteropolysaccharide, the introduction of anion functional groups and the tendency to a rigid solution conformation improved the bioactivities of anti-tumor (Liu et al., 2021) and immunomodulatory (Li et al., 2020). Moreover, compared with homopolysaccharide, heteropolysaccharide with diverse monosaccharide components and more branches resulting in critical problem of low substrate solubility, thereby leading to low subsequent conversion efficiency and harsh reaction environment. This is particularly evident in conventional polysaccharide selenylation systems, thus making the solvent as a key entry point for the construction of novel polysaccharide selenylation system (Guo et al., 2017). It has been demonstrated in many works that the hydrogen bond property of DES contributes to providing more hydrogen bonding sites, which is beneficial to break the hydrogen bond networks and promote the solubilization and subsequent functionalization reactions of polysaccharide (Cao et al., 2019). However, there is a relative paucity of empirical research specifically addressing the feasibility of DES for dissolving heteropolysaccharide and the effect of solvent composition regulation on dissolution capacity. For the highly solvent-dependent heteropolysaccharide processing, it is necessary to explore the prospect of DES as an effective solvent and reaction medium in the rather difficult selenylation reaction and expand the applicability of DES in the field of polysaccharide functionalization.

Artemisia sphaerocephala is a kind of sand-fixing plant widely distributed in northwest China, and a branched heteropolysaccharide extracted from its seeds (PAS) showed a weight average molecular mass (M_w) of 6.96 × 10^4 g/mol (Wei et al., 2019). In this work, in order to break the bottleneck caused by heteropolysaccharide solubility limita- tion, a DES-mediated solvent system for PAS was proposed, and further quantum chemical calculations were used to investigate the interactions within mono and binary solvents systems to speculate the possible sol- ubility mechanism. Then, efficient DES-mediated Se-functionalizations of PAS and corresponding structural confirmations were carried out to explore the effect of this selenylation system on the conversion effi- ciency and heteropolysaccharide chain features. It is hoped that this research will contribute to a deeper understanding regarding the effect of DES on heteropolysaccharide solubilization and provide a reference for the investigation of DES performance modulation in biomolecular functionalization.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), choline chloride (ChCl), tetramethylammonium chloride (TMAC), ethylene glycol (EG), urea, glycerin (GLY), 1,4-butanediol (BDO), trifluoroacetic acid, hydroxylamine hydrochloride, pyridine, chloroform, Reichardt's dye (30) (RD), N,N-dimethyl-4-nitroaniline (DMNA), 4-nitroaniline (NA), ascorbic acid, potassium bromide (KBr), 2,3-diaminonaphthalene (DAN), ethylenediamine tetraacetate (EDTA-2Na), congo red (CR) and methylene blue (MB) were purchased from Jingchun Industry Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China. All chemicals used in present work were analytical reagents or better grades with no further purification.
PAS was extracted and purified according to our previous study (Wei et al., 2019). In brief, crude PAS was extracted with distilled water at

80 °C for 18 h. All extraction solution was concentrated and then deproteinated using Sevag method to obtain purified PAS with M_W of 6.96 × 10^4 g/mol. The monosaccharide compositions of PAS were L-arabinose (Ara), D-xylose (Xyl), D-mannose (Man), D-glucose (Glc) and D-galactose (Gal) in molar ratio of 1: 4.33: 3.21: 4.63: 2.57.

2.2. Preparation of DESs DESs were prepared by mixing the HBAs with the corresponding HBDs according to the molar ratios provided in Table 1, and all the relevant materials had been dried prior to preparation. The mixture in the sealed flask was stirred with a magnetic stirrer and heated at 80 °C until clear homogenous liquid was obtained. Heated for another 2 h, the mixture was placed in a glass vial and kept in a vacuum chamber at 50 °C to remove moisture from DES, then stored the glass vial in a desiccator to prevent moisture absorption.

2.3. Polarity determination of DESs The polarity scale ($E_T^N$), dipolarity/polarizability ($\pi^*$), hydrogen bond acidity ($\alpha$) and hydrogen bond basicity ($\beta$) were calculated according to modified Kamlet-Taft empirical polarity scales ([Ranjkesh et al., 2018](https://www.google.com/search?q=Ranjkesh+et+al.,+2018)). $E_T(30)/\text{kcal}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} = 28591/\lambda_{\text{max(RD)}}$ (1) $E_T^N/\text{kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} = (E_T(30) - 30.7)/32.4$ (2) $\pi^* = (28.18 - \nu_{\text{(DMNA)}})/3.52$ (3) $\beta = (0.9841 \times \nu_{\text{(DMNA)}} + 3.49 - \nu_{\text{(NA)}})/2.759$ (4) $\alpha = (E_T(30) - 31.2 - 11.5\pi^*)/15.2$ (5) where, $\nu_{\text{(NA)}} = 1/(\lambda_{\text{max(NA)}} \times 10^{-4})\text{kK}$ (6) $\nu_{\text{(DMNA)}} = 1/(\lambda_{\text{max(DMNA)}} \times 10^{-4})\text{kK}$ (7) Here, $\lambda_{\text{max(RD)}}$ [nm] represented the maximum absorption wavelength of Reichardt's dye (30). $\lambda_{\text{max(NA)}}$ [nm] and $\lambda_{\text{max(DMNA)}}$ [nm] represented the maximum absorption wavelength of 4-nitroaniline and N, N-dimethyl-4-nitroaniline.

2.4. Measurement of viscosity The viscosity was measured using Physica MCR 301 rheometer (Anton Paar, Austria) with a 50 mm parallel plate (PP50). Solvent viscosity measurement was performed at temperatures ranging from 20 °C to 95 °C at 10 °C intervals. Shear-dependence viscosity of solvent was measured at 25 °C and 80 °C in a shear rate range between 0.1 and 100 s-1.

2.5. Solubility of PAS in different solvents The detailed measurement procedure was according to a recent study (Cao et al., 2019). Briefly, PAS was accurately weighed (5 g ± 0.1 mg) into different solvents (10 g ± 0.1 mg) and the mixture was magnetically stirred at 80 °C for 5 h. The dissolved samples were centrifuged at 10000 rpm for 30 min, and the supernatant was collected. The super- natant was diluted 50 times with deionised water, then 1 mL of deion- ised water and 1 mL of 6% (w/v) phenol were added and mixed well. Next, 5 mL of concentrated sulfuric acid was added to the mixture and mixed well. After standing for 30 min, the absorption spectrum of the mixture at 490 nm was measured and calculated according to the following equation:

S=(A490nm-b)/a × 0.9 × 10 (8) where S represented the solubility of PAS (g/100 g), the absorbance of the mixture at 490 nm was expressed as A490nm, the slope and intercept of the standard curve were expressed as a and b. The standard curve was obtained by dissolving 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5 g of glucose into 10 g of different DESs according to the above procedure. The determination process was performed in triplicate. The experimental data were analyzed using SPSS V.17.0 (p < 0.05).

2.6. *Polarized light microscope* 0.25 g PAS was put into 50 g solvent and stirred at 80 °C for 5 h. One drop of solution was transferred onto the slide and covered with coverslip. The polarized light microscopy (Axio scope A1, Carl Zeiss, Germany) was performed to observe PAS granules and capture images.

## 2.7. Computational methods The initial structure optimization of DES was performed at HF/6-311G(d,p) level, and further reoptimization was obtained using the M06-2X exchange-correlation function in combination the 6-31++G(d,p) basis set based on the Gaussian 16 program package (Zhao & Truhlar, 2008). In order to reveal the non-covalent interactions in DES and DES/DMSO systems, the reduced density gradients (RDG) was calculated using Multiwfn program and the data were visualized by VMD and Gnuplot (Lu & Chen, 2012a). The electrostatic surface potential (ESP) of molecule was used to analyze hydrogen bond interactions, and the locations of the surface extrema and the statistical analysis of van der Waals (vdW) surface area in different ESP ranges were calculated referring to previous works (Lu & Chen, 2012b; Lu & Manzetti, 2014). For atoms in molecules (AIM) analysis, the electron density and Laplace amount of electron density at the bond critical point (BCP), namely ρ(BCP) and ∇²ρ(BCP), were commonly used to analyze the bond strength as well as covalent character (Lu & Chen, 2013). The reactivity of the solvent system was further analyzed by frontline molecular orbitals (FMO) theory in combination with Multiwfn program and VMD.

## 2.8. Se-functionalization of PAS The preparation of Se-functionalized PAS (SePAS) was achieved according to the previously reported method (Tao et al., 2021; Xiao et al., 2019) with some modifications. To ensure the same reaction environment volume, the pure DES reaction volume was 60 mL, and the mixed solvents consisted of 30 mL DES and 30 mL DMSO. The above solvents were separately placed in three neck vials. PAS (300 mg) was added into the vial at 80 °C while stirring in oil bath for 5 h. Next, H2SeO3 (1.25 g) was added and stirred at 80 °C for 5 h under nitrogen atmosphere. After the reaction was complete, the sample was centrifuged at 10000 rpm for 10 min. The collected supernatant was dialyzed with distilled water for 48 h (molecular mass cut-off 5–8 kDa) until the solution was colorless when ascorbic acid was added. Finally, the mixture was centrifuged at
8000 rpm for 5 min. The collected supernatant was evaporated, precipitated with acetone and lyophilized for 48 h to obtain SePAS.

2.9. FT-IR spectra The powdery samples were prepared by grinding mixture of 1 mg of sample with 200 mg of dried KBr and pressing into slices. The liquid samples were prepared by liquid films method using KBr slices. The spectra were recorded at the wavenumber range of 4000–400 cm⁻¹ with FT-IR spectrophotometer (iS10, Thermo Nicolet, USA). The number of scans was 16 and referenced against air. The resolution of FT-IR was 4 cm⁻¹.

2.10. *NMR analysis* 1H, 13C, 1H–1H COSY and 1H–13C HSQC NMR spectra were recorded at 25 °C by a Bruker Avance DPX-400 spectrometer (Bruker, Rheinstetten, Germany). Chemical shifts were reported in ppm using TMS as the internal reference. The NMR spectra of DESs and polysaccharides were determined in DMSO-d6 and D₂O, respectively.

2.11. Determination of selenium content The selenium contents of SePASs were determined as described in our previous study (Wei et al., 2019). The mixture of 2 mL of acid (H2SO4: HNO3: HClO4=1:1:4, V/V) was used to hydrolyze the sample in microwave digestion system (Multiwave 3000, Anton Paar, Austria) for 1.5 h. After cooling, the digestion solution was concentrated to 2 mL and 8 mL of 0.1 mol/L hydrochloric acid was added. To the mixed so- lution, added 4 mL of 0.5 mol/L hydroxylamine hydrochloride and 0.2 mol/L EDTA-2Na, mixing well and standing for 10 min. Then added 2 mL of 0.1% DAN solution and placed it in dark place for storage. The mixture was boiled in water bath for 5 min and then cooled and extracted with 5 mL of cyclohexane. Fluorescence spectrometry (RF- 5301PC, Shimadzu, Japan) was used for detecting the fluorescence in- tensity of cyclohexane solution (excitation and emission wavelength at 376 and 520 nm, respectively). The selenium content in the sample was calculated from the standard curve.

2.12. Molecular mass analysis The molecular mass of the sample (1 mg/mL) was determined via size-exclusion chromatography combined with multi-angle laser light scattering (SEC-MALLS). The sample was filtered through a 0.45 µm cellulose filter and eluted by a Ultrahydrogel TM column (7.8 x 300 mm, Waters, USA) with ultrapure water as mobile phase. The injection volume and flow rate were 50 µL and 0.5 mL/min, respectively. The refractive index increment (dn/dc) value was determined to be 0.145 mL/g. Zimm method was used to calculate the Mw and data analysis was performed using Astra software (Wyatt Tech. Corp., USA).

2.13. SePAS/dye interaction analysis 2 mL of each polysaccharide solution with different concentrations (0.01-0.2 mg/mL) was added to 2 mL of MB solution (0.02 mg/mL) at room temperature respectively. After shaking at 70 °C for 10 min, the solution was warmed up to 90 °C and then shaken for 20 min in water bath. The absorption spectra were performed after cooling (UV1000, Labtech, China). 2 mL of polysaccharide solution (0.02-0.5 mg/mL) was mixed well with 2 mL of CR dye (91 µg/mL) at room temperature. In addition, 2 mL of NaOH solution (0.1-2 mg/mL) was added to 4 mL of polysaccharide (0.2 mg/mL)/CR mixed solution, and the absorption spectra of the above samples were recorded in the range of 300-700 nm (UV1000, Labtech, China).

## 2.14. Monosaccharide composition analysis The sample (10 mg) was hydrolyzed with trifluoroacetic acid under nitrogen protection at 120 °C for 8 h. The residual trifluoroacetic acid was removed by rotary evaporation. The hydrolysis product was added with ammonium hydrochloride (10 mg) and pyridine (1 mL) and reacted at 90 °C for 30 min. After cooling to room temperature, 1 mL of acetic anhydride was added and reacted at 90 °C for 30 min. The final product was extracted with 1 mL of chloroform and filtered through a 0.22 µm filter. The ensuing analysis was conducted by GC–MS (Polaris-Q, Thermo, USA) according to our previous study (Wei et al., 2019).

## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. Characterization of hydrogen bond interactions in DESs As shown in Fig. 1a, the FT-IR spectra for HBAs, HBDs and the corresponding DESs were compared to prove hydrogen bond interactions. In DES$_{1-4}$, hydroxyl group stretching vibration was observed at 3333, 3347, 3354 and 3335 cm⁻¹ respectively, which showed blue shifts compared with ChCl (3255 cm⁻¹). Similarly, it could be noted that asymmetric stretching vibrations of the methyl in TMAC were at 2914 cm⁻¹, which shifted to 2969 cm⁻¹ for DES₅. On the other hand, the absorption peaks with strong intensity at 3357, 3374, and 3325 cm⁻¹ were attributed to hydroxyl group stretching vibration of the polyol HBDs (EG, GLY and BDO), which exhibited absorption peaks shifts when DESs were formed. These findings indicated the intermolecular hydrogen bond interactions between HBA and HBD. It was supported that the addition of HBD weakened the intermolecular hydrogen bonds of ChCl itself, which caused the blue shift effect of hydroxyl group stretching vibration of ChCl, demonstrating the formation of hydrogen bonds between HBA and HBD (Wang et al., 2019). The study reported by Hou et al. also demonstrated that the forming of strong hydrogen bonds resulted in hydroxyl group stretching vibration of HBD shifting from 3331 to 3218 cm⁻¹ (Hou et al., 2015).
The hydrogen bond interactions between HBA and HBD were further investigated via ¹H NMR spectra of DES₁₋₈ (Fig. 1c). It was apparent that

compared with HBA or HBD, the active hydrogen signal in corre-sponding DES upshifted for HBA and downshifted for HBD, which confirmed the existence of hydrogen bond interactions. As shown in Fig. S2, the chemical shift at 5.74 and 5.68 ppm corresponded to hy-droxyl group of ChCl and hydrogen atoms of urea, which shifted to 5.52 and 5.87 ppm in ChCl-Urea, respectively. This result might be explained by the fact that the formation of intermolecular hydrogen bonds be-tween ChCl and urea weakened the interactions between chloridion and hydroxyl group within ChCl, thus increasing the electron density of hydroxyl group and causing the chemical shift moving to high field. Meanwhile, hydroxyl group contributed to providing hydrogen bonding site resulting in the hydroxyl group signal of BDO shifting from 4.47 to 4.52 ppm in TMAC-BDO (Fig. S2). This result could be explained by the fact that the formation of hydrogen bonds caused the electron density of hydrogen atom in hydroxyl group reduction, which leading to the downshift of chemical shift (Hao et al., 2017). These findings matched the observation in previous studies that upshifting of the active hydrogen signal in HBA (tetraethylammonium hydroxide, from 0.91 to 0.74 ppm) and downshifting in HBD (GLY, from 3.681 to 3.798 ppm) (Sirviö & Heiskanen, 2020; Zaid et al., 2017). Overall, the results in this section indicated that hydrogen bonds formed between HBA and HBD.

The high polarities of the ChCl-based DESs might be related to the existence of charged polar functional groups in the asymmetric chemical structure of ChCl (Florindo et al., 2018), which was beneficial to the dissociation of anions and cations, thus improving the activity of ions such as chloride ions (Ren et al., 2016). Further, an attempt was made to explore the driving forces and important influences behind the dissolution of PAS by DESs from the perspective of quantified hydrogen bond interactions through quantum chemistry calculations. The system structures and optimized conformations of ChCl-Urea, TMAC-Urea, ChCl-Urea/DMSO and TMAC-Urea/ DMSO were shown in Fig. 2. It could be seen from the optimized geometries that the multiple active electronegative atoms and hydroxyl groups in the HBAs and HBDs structures conferred the ability to conduct hydrogen bonding interactions. And these atomic spacings were proven to be all within the acceptable criteria for hydrogen bond coordination (< 3.5 Å).

Molecular electrostatic potential was a valid means for analyzing and predicting hydrogen bond interactions and was applied here to analyze the contributing effect of PAS solubility in DES. Further, the positive and negative average values of ESP could quantitatively provide information related to the solubility of the condensed phase that depended on non-covalent interactions (Murray & Politzer, 2011). As shown in the data of ESP analysis, the solubility of PAS presented a certain positive relationship with the corresponding overall average ESP value of each DES. ChCl-Urea had the largest overall average value of ESP (3.92 kcal/mol), and the plot of its surface area in each ESP range showed that the maximum area range (14.31%) was positive 32.67. This might contribute to stronger interactions between ChCl-Urea and PAS with

plenty of negative charge, thus improving the solubility of PAS. In addition, it could be seen from Fig. S4 that the overall average value of ESP in ChCl-BDO with lower dissolving capacity was only 0.86 kcal/ mol, the surface area distribution in different ESP range was relatively uneven, with the largest area (25.04%) of just positive 7.00. Similarly, the overall lower average electrostatic potential of TMAC-Urea might influence the interactions with the hydroxyl groups of polysaccharides, resulting in lesser solubility.

The possible dissolution mechanism of PAS in ChCl-Urea was pre-dicted by FMO analysis since the molecular orbitals were significant electronic parameters for describing the chemical reactivities of com-pounds. As shown in Fig. 3a, the highest occupied molecular orbitals (HOMO) electron cloud of ChCl-Urea was localized on chloridion, and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals (LUMO) electron cloud was mostly localized on the carbon and hydrogen atoms of the quaternary ammonium cation as well as the amino group of urea. These results could provide insights into forecasting the action sites between DES and PAS. It was well known that HOMO determined the region where elec-trons had the highest reaction energy, while LUMO established a region for filling with intruding electrons from other molecules during the bonding process (Dwamena & Raynie, 2020). Because of this, HOMO was related to the propensity to donate electrons, while LUMO was related to the propensity to accept electrons. Therefore, it was specu-lated that the LUMO region and HOMO region in ChCl-Urea might interact with the nucleophilic and potentiophilic sites in PAS, respec-tively. This finding was supported by the research of Zhang et al. that hydroxyl protons of cellulose could form strong hydrogen bonds with chloridions, and the intermolecular hydrogen bond networks of cellu-lose were broken during this process (Zhang et al., 2014).

According to the above solubility phenomena together with the theoretical calculations and analysis, the studied DESs were full of hydrogen bond interactions and the multiple hydrogen bonding sites within the system provided their abilities to interact with PAS. Effect of co-solvent effect on PAS dissolution In this work, considering the viscosity and cost of solvent in poly-saccharide functionalization, the common organic solvent DMSO was chosen to construct binary mixed solvents system, and further exploring the potential of the DES/DMSO system. This also corresponded to the increased hydrogen bond ba-sicity (β) of DES/DMSO system (Table S1), which promoted the in-teractions between mixed solvents and hydroxyl groups on polysaccharides, breaking the original polysaccharide hydrogen bond networks and creating new hydrogen bonds with polysaccharides (Tomimatsu et al., 2019). Similarly, Mai et al. reported that the [Bmim][Cl]/DMSO mixture with higher β value exhibited significantly enhanced lignocel-lulose dissolving capacity (Mai et al., 2014). In addition, FT-IR was performed on regenerated PAS from binary mixed solvents, and there was no significant difference in the characteristic peaks between the untreated and regenerated PASs. There were no significant changes observed in the composition and molar ratio of monosaccharides in the regenerated polysaccharides compared to PAS (Fig. S5). 3.4. Se-functionalization of PAS promoted by hydrogen bond modulation In this work, with the purpose of constructing a novel polysaccharide functionalization system, PAS was firstly Se-functionalized in the reaction system with DES as the solvent, while related control experiments were carried out under different solvent conditions at the same time. Table 2 presented selenium contents and yields of SePASs obtained under different conditions. Due to the weak solubility of PAS in DMSO (Fig. 2a), the selenium content of SePASDMSO (970.98 µg/g) obtained by the selenylation reaction conducted in DMSO were significantly lower. When DESs as reaction media, the selenium contents of corresponding SePASDES₁ and SePASDES₂ were elevated to 1535.60 and 2126.70 μg/g, respectively. It indicated that adequate solubilization of polysaccharide had a significant impact on determining the efficiency of subsequent functionalization. DES exhibited the dual properties of hydrogen bond providing and accepting abilities, and this characteristic brought about the superior solubilizing capacity of DES, which was supported by the above experimental and computational analysis. Therefore, it was probable that DES could break the hydrogen bond interactions between polysaccharide chains and expose more hydroxyl groups. In addition, the high viscosity of ChCl-Urea impeded the contact of substrates in the reaction system under sufficient solubilization condition, resulting in a compromised selenylation efficiency of SePASDES₁. The excellent dissolving capacity and lower viscosity of ChCl-EG might cause the seleno-groups to be more easily introduced into the polysaccharide chains, thus enhancing the efficiency of the selenylation reaction. Consequently, DES with multiple hydrogen bonding sites was capable of being a new type of selenylation medium.

On the basis of the promising Se-functionalization effect of DES system, the co-solvent effect on the selenylation efficiency of PAS in DES/DMSO binary mixed solvents system was further explored. The selenium contents of SePAS₁ and SePAS₂ were 1947.46 and 4004.29 µg/g, which increased to a certain extent compared with the corresponding SePASDES₁ (1535.60 µg/g) and SePASDES₂ (2126.70 µg/g) obtained in pure DES systems. As shown in Fig. S6, the co-solvent strategy could reduce the viscosity of the reaction system and facilitate the contact between polysaccharides and H₂SeO₃ (Damstrup et al., 2006). Additionally, the binary mixed solvents system was shown in theoretical calculations and analysis to provide more hydrogen bonding sites in interaction with PAS (Section 3.3), allowing adequate exposure of PAS hydroxyl groups. The combination of the above two factors could lead to a better nucleophilic attack by hydroxyl groups, thus favoring the polysaccharide selenylation reaction. Similarly, Harifi-Mood et al. studied the reaction of 1-fluoro-2,4-dinitrobenzene with piperidine in DES/DMSO binary mixed solvents and found that the increase of DMSO was beneficial to elevate the reaction rate (Harifi-Mood & Sadrzadeh, 2018). Moreover, selenium contents of SePAS₁₋₈ were higher than that of SePASc (1703.00 µg/g) obtained by conventional system (HNO₃-H₂SeO₃) (Wang, Zhao, et al., 2012). This valuable result

SePAS1–8 had a certain correlation with the polarity of the corre- sponding DES/DMSO, and the overall rule presented a trend that the higher polarity (higher $E_T^N$ value) of DES/DMSO, the lower $M_W$ of sele- nium polysaccharide. This relationship was likely to be related to the fact that high polarity solvent was more conducive to the dissociation of anions and cations, which was beneficial to the destruction of hydrogen bonds within polysaccharide chains by chloridion and the subsequent major degradation of polysaccharide chains by acidic reaction envi- ronment. This also corresponded to the finding that both solubility and selenium content showed a correlation with polarity of DES. Likewise, the study of Liu et al. reported that the hydrogen bonds between chloride ions of DES and hydroxyl groups might weaken the strong hydrogen bond interactions in wood lignocellulose, thus breaking lignin- carbohydrate complexes linkages (Liu et al., 2017).

Furthermore, the evolution of chain conformation in polysaccharide Se-functionalization mediated by DES/DMSO was investigated using MB and CR spectrophotometric method (Prentø, 2001). With increasing SePAS2 concentration, the gradual decrease at OD664nm of MB/SePAS2 absorption spectra and the progressive increase at OD554nm indicated that the positively charged MB interacted with the negatively charged SePAS2, which proved that seleno-groups were successfully introduced (Fig. 6c). Following this interactions, a long-range forces involving water and MB molecules appeared to bring the planar cationic molecules relatively close to each other and form metachromatic complexes, leading to selenium polysaccharide more inclined to rigid conformation (Michon et al., 2002). Meanwhile, it was observed that when SePAS2 concentration was 0.2 mg/mL, a large increase in NaOH destroyed the SePAS2/CR electrostatic interactions and disrupted the tendency for λmax of SePAS2/CR to be continuously red-shifting (Fig. 6d), which suggested that the rigid conformation of selenium polysaccharide (Tan et al., 2020). Similar results were reported by Liu et al. that the upward trend in λmax of polysaccharide/CR was influenced by the increasing NaOH concentration, confirming the extended conformation of polysaccharide (Liu et al., 2016).

According to the above results, it was found that the M_W of SePAS was related to the polarity of DES, owing to the positive contribution of the high polarity DES to destruct the hydrogen bond networks of poly- saccharides, which further affected the degradation of polysaccharides by acid environment. Additionally, the DES/DMSO-mediated introduc- tion of seleno-group rendered the polysaccharide chains towards more rigid conformation. In summary, it might be possible to prospectively modulate the selenylation efficiency and polysaccharide M_W simulta- neously by constructing task-specific DESs with different HBAs/HBDs and solvent properties, which also provided new perspectives for the selection of solvent systems for polysaccharide derivatization reactions.

## 4. Conclusion The DES/DMSO binary solvents with more and stronger hydrogen bonding sites could coordinate the disruption and reconstruction of hydrogen bonds within polysaccharides, attaining superior solubilization ability than DES. The polysaccharide hydroxyl groups were fully exposed and activated in DES/DMSO-mediated novel Se-functionalization system owing to the disruption of the hydrogen bond networks, which facilitated selenylation efficiency and rendered acid-dependent M_w reduction. The obtained SePAS presented a tendency of rigid conformation due to the introduction of anion functional groups. In summary, this study supported further development of DESs with regulable solvent properties towards solubilization and functionalization high-value exploitation of heteropolysaccharide bioresources.

This revealed that choline chloride-based DES/DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide) binary mixed solvents possessed more and stronger hydrogen bonding sites, facilitating the balance between disruption and reconstruction of hydrogen bonds within branched heteropolysaccharide from *Artemisia sphaerocephala* (PAS) and achieving efficient solubilization. Further, due to the full exposure and activation of polysaccharide hydroxyls, the efficiency of DES/ DMSO-mediated novel Se-functionalization was substantially enhanced compared to the conventional selenylation methods. The derivative exhibited conversion to lower molecular mass with rigid solution conformation based on co-solvent effect and predominant acidic environment influence. This study offered a framework for exploring the potential of individualized polysaccharide functionalization by modulating DES constituents to achieve multiple controllabilities in terms of conversion efficiency and derivative structure. # 1. Introduction The ever increasing demands for resources in modern society and the promotion of environmental protection have led to a growing global concern for sustainable natural biological resource (Xu, Che, et al., 2019). In particular, polysaccharide resources of natural biological origin have been used in fuels, materials and pharmaceuticals (Mika et al., 2018). Limitations of structural properties make many natural polysaccharides biologically inactive, hence functionalization strategy becomes an effective way to develop polysaccharide resources (Li et al., 2016). However, owing to the complex structures and the presence of multiple hydrogen bond networks of polysaccharides, organic solvents that mediate polysaccharides functionalization in traditional reaction systems present poor abilities to dissolve polysaccharides and draw-backs such as wastewater contamination and biological toxicity (Farrán et al., 2015). The resulting non-homogeneous environment generally leads to reduced functionalization efficiencies of polysaccharides, which is not conducive to the exploitation of biological resources. Accordingly, the functionalized valorized development of natural resources requires new solvents and reaction media to achieve the mutual promotion and coordination between the efficient utilization of resources and ecolog- ical environmental protection. Green solvents are a class of environmentally friendly solvents that have been widely used in the development of biological resources in recent years, among which deep eutectic solvents (DESs) prepared by the hydrogen bond interactions between hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) and hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) are considered to possess great potential for macromolecular biotransformation (Hansen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2012). The hydrogen bond providing/accepting ability of DESs can break hydrogen bonds between carbohydrates, while DESs exhibit high designability, low toxicity and low volatility (Chen & Mu, 2019). At the same time, the high viscosity and thermal decompo- sition exhibited by parts of DESs (González-Rivera et al., 2020; Rodri- guez Rodriguez et al., 2019) make the application of DESs to the processing of natural polysaccharides full of opportunities and chal- lenges. Moreover, the great dissolving performance of DES for poly- saccharide could be enhanced by building binary mixed solvents system to further reduce the viscosity, leading to lower experimental cost and * Corresponding author at: College of Life Science, Northwest Normal University, Anning Eastroad, Lanzhou, People's Republic of China. The dual solvent-solute/solvent interac- tion existing in the mixed solvents can further affect the reaction effi- ciency via solvent effects (Reichardt & Welton, 2011; Ruan et al., 2021). Hereby, much attention has been paid to investigating the interaction between co-solvents and DESs as well as the effect of modulating sol- vents on the functionalization of polysaccharide resources. Se-functionalization is an important approach to enhance the activity of natural polysaccharides and has been widely reported in recent years as a promising modification of natural polysaccharides (Li et al., 2019; Xu, Wu, et al., 2019). Our previous works achieved selenylation of natural heteropolysaccharide and revealed that in case of modified heteropolysaccharide, the introduction of anion functional groups and the tendency to a rigid solution conformation improved the bioactivities of anti-tumor (Liu et al., 2021) and immunomodulatory (Li et al., 2020). Moreover, compared with homopolysaccharide, heteropolysaccharide with diverse monosaccharide components and more branches resulting in critical problem of low substrate solubility, thereby leading to low subsequent conversion efficiency and harsh reaction environment. This is particularly evident in conventional polysaccharide selenylation systems, thus making the solvent as a key entry point for the construction of novel polysaccharide selenylation system (Guo et al., 2017). It has been demonstrated in many works that the hydrogen bond property of DES contributes to providing more hydrogen bonding sites, which is beneficial to break the hydrogen bond networks and promote the solubilization and subsequent functionalization reactions of polysaccharide (Cao et al., 2019). However, there is a relative paucity of empirical research specifically addressing the feasibility of DES for dissolving heteropolysaccharide and the effect of solvent composition regulation on dissolution capacity. For the highly solvent-dependent heteropolysaccharide processing, it is necessary to explore the prospect of DES as an effective solvent and reaction medium in the rather difficult selenylation reaction and expand the applicability of DES in the field of polysaccharide functionalization. Artemisia sphaerocephala is a kind of sand-fixing plant widely distributed in northwest China, and a branched heteropolysaccharide extracted from its seeds (PAS) showed a weight average molecular mass (M_w) of 6.96 × 10^4 g/mol (Wei et al., 2019). In this work, in order to break the bottleneck caused by heteropolysaccharide solubility limita- tion, a DES-mediated solvent system for PAS was proposed, and further quantum chemical calculations were used to investigate the interactions within mono and binary solvents systems to speculate the possible sol- ubility mechanism. Then, efficient DES-mediated Se-functionalizations of PAS and corresponding structural confirmations were carried out to explore the effect of this selenylation system on the conversion effi- ciency and heteropolysaccharide chain features. It is hoped that this research will contribute to a deeper understanding regarding the effect of DES on heteropolysaccharide solubilization and provide a reference for the investigation of DES performance modulation in biomolecular functionalization. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), choline chloride (ChCl), tetramethylammonium chloride (TMAC), ethylene glycol (EG), urea, glycerin (GLY), 1,4-butanediol (BDO), trifluoroacetic acid, hydroxylamine hydrochloride, pyridine, chloroform, Reichardt's dye (30) (RD), N,N-dimethyl-4-nitroaniline (DMNA), 4-nitroaniline (NA), ascorbic acid, potassium bromide (KBr), 2,3-diaminonaphthalene (DAN), ethylenediamine tetraacetate (EDTA-2Na), congo red (CR) and methylene blue (MB) were purchased from Jingchun Industry Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China. All chemicals used in present work were analytical reagents or better grades with no further purification. PAS was extracted and purified according to our previous study (Wei et al., 2019). In brief, crude PAS was extracted with distilled water at 80 °C for 18 h. All extraction solution was concentrated and then deproteinated using Sevag method to obtain purified PAS with M_W of 6.96 × 10^4 g/mol. The monosaccharide compositions of PAS were L-arabinose (Ara), D-xylose (Xyl), D-mannose (Man), D-glucose (Glc) and D-galactose (Gal) in molar ratio of 1: 4.33: 3.21: 4.63: 2.57. 2.2. Preparation of DESs DESs were prepared by mixing the HBAs with the corresponding HBDs according to the molar ratios provided in Table 1, and all the relevant materials had been dried prior to preparation. The mixture in the sealed flask was stirred with a magnetic stirrer and heated at 80 °C until clear homogenous liquid was obtained. Heated for another 2 h, the mixture was placed in a glass vial and kept in a vacuum chamber at 50 °C to remove moisture from DES, then stored the glass vial in a desiccator to prevent moisture absorption. 2.3. Polarity determination of DESs The polarity scale ($E_T^N$), dipolarity/polarizability ($\pi^*$), hydrogen bond acidity ($\alpha$) and hydrogen bond basicity ($\beta$) were calculated according to modified Kamlet-Taft empirical polarity scales ([Ranjkesh et al., 2018](https://www.google.com/search?q=Ranjkesh+et+al.,+2018)). $E_T(30)/\text{kcal}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} = 28591/\lambda_{\text{max(RD)}}$ (1) $E_T^N/\text{kJ}\cdot\text{mol}^{-1} = (E_T(30) - 30.7)/32.4$ (2) $\pi^* = (28.18 - \nu_{\text{(DMNA)}})/3.52$ (3) $\beta = (0.9841 \times \nu_{\text{(DMNA)}} + 3.49 - \nu_{\text{(NA)}})/2.759$ (4) $\alpha = (E_T(30) - 31.2 - 11.5\pi^*)/15.2$ (5) where, $\nu_{\text{(NA)}} = 1/(\lambda_{\text{max(NA)}} \times 10^{-4})\text{kK}$ (6) $\nu_{\text{(DMNA)}} = 1/(\lambda_{\text{max(DMNA)}} \times 10^{-4})\text{kK}$ (7) Here, $\lambda_{\text{max(RD)}}$ [nm] represented the maximum absorption wavelength of Reichardt's dye (30). $\lambda_{\text{max(NA)}}$ [nm] and $\lambda_{\text{max(DMNA)}}$ [nm] represented the maximum absorption wavelength of 4-nitroaniline and N, N-dimethyl-4-nitroaniline. 2.4. Measurement of viscosity The viscosity was measured using Physica MCR 301 rheometer (Anton Paar, Austria) with a 50 mm parallel plate (PP50). Solvent viscosity measurement was performed at temperatures ranging from 20 °C to 95 °C at 10 °C intervals. Briefly, PAS was accurately weighed (5 g ± 0.1 mg) into different solvents (10 g ± 0.1 mg) and the mixture was magnetically stirred at 80 °C for 5 h. The dissolved samples were centrifuged at 10000 rpm for 30 min, and the supernatant was collected. The super- natant was diluted 50 times with deionised water, then 1 mL of deion- ised water and 1 mL of 6% (w/v) phenol were added and mixed well. Next, 5 mL of concentrated sulfuric acid was added to the mixture and mixed well. After standing for 30 min, the absorption spectrum of the mixture at 490 nm was measured and calculated according to the following equation: S=(A490nm-b)/a × 0.9 × 10 (8) where S represented the solubility of PAS (g/100 g), the absorbance of the mixture at 490 nm was expressed as A490nm, the slope and intercept of the standard curve were expressed as a and b. The standard curve was obtained by dissolving 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5 g of glucose into 10 g of different DESs according to the above procedure. The determination process was performed in triplicate. The experimental data were analyzed using SPSS V.17.0 (p < 0.05). 2.6. *Polarized light microscope* 0.25 g PAS was put into 50 g solvent and stirred at 80 °C for 5 h. One drop of solution was transferred onto the slide and covered with coverslip. The polarized light microscopy (Axio scope A1, Carl Zeiss, Germany) was performed to observe PAS granules and capture images. ## 2.7. Computational methods The initial structure optimization of DES was performed at HF/6-311G(d,p) level, and further reoptimization was obtained using the M06-2X exchange-correlation function in combination the 6-31++G(d,p) basis set based on the Gaussian 16 program package (Zhao & Truhlar, 2008). In order to reveal the non-covalent interactions in DES and DES/DMSO systems, the reduced density gradients (RDG) was calculated using Multiwfn program and the data were visualized by VMD and Gnuplot (Lu & Chen, 2012a). The electrostatic surface potential (ESP) of molecule was used to analyze hydrogen bond interactions, and the locations of the surface extrema and the statistical analysis of van der Waals (vdW) surface area in different ESP ranges were calculated referring to previous works (Lu & Chen, 2012b; Lu & Manzetti, 2014). For atoms in molecules (AIM) analysis, the electron density and Laplace amount of electron density at the bond critical point (BCP), namely ρ(BCP) and ∇²ρ(BCP), were commonly used to analyze the bond strength as well as covalent character (Lu & Chen, 2013). The reactivity of the solvent system was further analyzed by frontline molecular orbitals (FMO) theory in combination with Multiwfn program and VMD. ## 2.8. Se-functionalization of PAS The preparation of Se-functionalized PAS (SePAS) was achieved according to the previously reported method (Tao et al., 2021; Xiao et al., 2019) with some modifications. To ensure the same reaction environment volume, the pure DES reaction volume was 60 mL, and the mixed solvents consisted of 30 mL DES and 30 mL DMSO. The above solvents were separately placed in three neck vials. PAS (300 mg) was added into the vial at 80 °C while stirring in oil bath for 5 h. Next, H2SeO3 (1.25 g) was added and stirred at 80 °C for 5 h under nitrogen atmosphere. After the reaction was complete, the sample was centrifuged at 10000 rpm for 10 min. The collected supernatant was dialyzed with distilled water for 48 h (molecular mass cut-off 5–8 kDa) until the solution was colorless when ascorbic acid was added. Finally, the mixture was centrifuged at 8000 rpm for 5 min. The collected supernatant was evaporated, precipitated with acetone and lyophilized for 48 h to obtain SePAS. 2.9. FT-IR spectra The powdery samples were prepared by grinding mixture of 1 mg of sample with 200 mg of dried KBr and pressing into slices. The liquid samples were prepared by liquid films method using KBr slices. The spectra were recorded at the wavenumber range of 4000–400 cm⁻¹ with FT-IR spectrophotometer (iS10, Thermo Nicolet, USA). The number of scans was 16 and referenced against air. The resolution of FT-IR was 4 cm⁻¹. 2.10. *NMR analysis* 1H, 13C, 1H–1H COSY and 1H–13C HSQC NMR spectra were recorded at 25 °C by a Bruker Avance DPX-400 spectrometer (Bruker, Rheinstetten, Germany). Chemical shifts were reported in ppm using TMS as the internal reference. The NMR spectra of DESs and polysaccharides were determined in DMSO-d6 and D₂O, respectively. 2.11. Determination of selenium content The selenium contents of SePASs were determined as described in our previous study (Wei et al., 2019). The mixture of 2 mL of acid (H2SO4: HNO3: HClO4=1:1:4, V/V) was used to hydrolyze the sample in microwave digestion system (Multiwave 3000, Anton Paar, Austria) for 1.5 h. After cooling, the digestion solution was concentrated to 2 mL and 8 mL of 0.1 mol/L hydrochloric acid was added. To the mixed so- lution, added 4 mL of 0.5 mol/L hydroxylamine hydrochloride and 0.2 mol/L EDTA-2Na, mixing well and standing for 10 min. Then added 2 mL of 0.1% DAN solution and placed it in dark place for storage. The mixture was boiled in water bath for 5 min and then cooled and extracted with 5 mL of cyclohexane. Fluorescence spectrometry (RF- 5301PC, Shimadzu, Japan) was used for detecting the fluorescence in- tensity of cyclohexane solution (excitation and emission wavelength at 376 and 520 nm, respectively). The selenium content in the sample was calculated from the standard curve. 2.12. Molecular mass analysis The molecular mass of the sample (1 mg/mL) was determined via size-exclusion chromatography combined with multi-angle laser light scattering (SEC-MALLS). The sample was filtered through a 0.45 µm cellulose filter and eluted by a Ultrahydrogel TM column (7.8 x 300 mm, Waters, USA) with ultrapure water as mobile phase. The injection volume and flow rate were 50 µL and 0.5 mL/min, respectively. The refractive index increment (dn/dc) value was determined to be 0.145 mL/g. Zimm method was used to calculate the Mw and data analysis was performed using Astra software (Wyatt Tech. Corp., USA). 2.13. SePAS/dye interaction analysis 2 mL of each polysaccharide solution with different concentrations (0.01-0.2 mg/mL) was added to 2 mL of MB solution (0.02 mg/mL) at room temperature respectively. After shaking at 70 °C for 10 min, the solution was warmed up to 90 °C and then shaken for 20 min in water bath. The absorption spectra were performed after cooling (UV1000, Labtech, China). 2 mL of polysaccharide solution (0.02-0.5 mg/mL) was mixed well with 2 mL of CR dye (91 µg/mL) at room temperature. In addition, 2 mL of NaOH solution (0.1-2 mg/mL) was added to 4 mL of polysaccharide (0.2 mg/mL)/CR mixed solution, and the absorption spectra of the above samples were recorded in the range of 300-700 nm (UV1000, Labtech, China). 3 Y. Monosaccharide composition analysis The sample (10 mg) was hydrolyzed with trifluoroacetic acid under nitrogen protection at 120 °C for 8 h. The residual trifluoroacetic acid was removed by rotary evaporation. The hydrolysis product was added with ammonium hydrochloride (10 mg) and pyridine (1 mL) and reacted at 90 °C for 30 min. After cooling to room temperature, 1 mL of acetic anhydride was added and reacted at 90 °C for 30 min. The final product was extracted with 1 mL of chloroform and filtered through a 0.22 µm filter. The ensuing analysis was conducted by GC–MS (Polaris-Q, Thermo, USA) according to our previous study (Wei et al., 2019). ## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. Characterization of hydrogen bond interactions in DESs As shown in Fig. 1a, the FT-IR spectra for HBAs, HBDs and the corresponding DESs were compared to prove hydrogen bond interactions. In DES$_{1-4}$, hydroxyl group stretching vibration was observed at 3333, 3347, 3354 and 3335 cm⁻¹ respectively, which showed blue shifts compared with ChCl (3255 cm⁻¹). Similarly, it could be noted that asymmetric stretching vibrations of the methyl in TMAC were at 2914 cm⁻¹, which shifted to 2969 cm⁻¹ for DES₅. On the other hand, the absorption peaks with strong intensity at 3357, 3374, and 3325 cm⁻¹ were attributed to hydroxyl group stretching vibration of the polyol HBDs (EG, GLY and BDO), which exhibited absorption peaks shifts when DESs were formed. These findings indicated the intermolecular hydrogen bond interactions between HBA and HBD. It was supported that the addition of HBD weakened the intermolecular hydrogen bonds of ChCl itself, which caused the blue shift effect of hydroxyl group stretching vibration of ChCl, demonstrating the formation of hydrogen bonds between HBA and HBD (Wang et al., 2019). The study reported by Hou et al. also demonstrated that the forming of strong hydrogen bonds resulted in hydroxyl group stretching vibration of HBD shifting from 3331 to 3218 cm⁻¹ (Hou et al., 2015). The hydrogen bond interactions between HBA and HBD were further investigated via ¹H NMR spectra of DES₁₋₈ (Fig. 1c). It was apparent that compared with HBA or HBD, the active hydrogen signal in corre-sponding DES upshifted for HBA and downshifted for HBD, which confirmed the existence of hydrogen bond interactions. As shown in Fig. S2, the chemical shift at 5.74 and 5.68 ppm corresponded to hy-droxyl group of ChCl and hydrogen atoms of urea, which shifted to 5.52 and 5.87 ppm in ChCl-Urea, respectively. This result might be explained by the fact that the formation of intermolecular hydrogen bonds be-tween ChCl and urea weakened the interactions between chloridion and hydroxyl group within ChCl, thus increasing the electron density of hydroxyl group and causing the chemical shift moving to high field. Meanwhile, hydroxyl group contributed to providing hydrogen bonding site resulting in the hydroxyl group signal of BDO shifting from 4.47 to 4.52 ppm in TMAC-BDO (Fig. S2). This result could be explained by the fact that the formation of hydrogen bonds caused the electron density of hydrogen atom in hydroxyl group reduction, which leading to the downshift of chemical shift (Hao et al., 2017). These findings matched the observation in previous studies that upshifting of the active hydrogen signal in HBA (tetraethylammonium hydroxide, from 0.91 to 0.74 ppm) and downshifting in HBD (GLY, from 3.681 to 3.798 ppm) (Sirviö & Heiskanen, 2020; Zaid et al., 2017). Overall, the results in this section indicated that hydrogen bonds formed between HBA and HBD. 3.2. Further, an attempt was made to explore the driving forces and important influences behind the dissolution of PAS by DESs from the perspective of quantified hydrogen bond interactions through quantum chemistry calculations. The system structures and optimized conformations of ChCl-Urea, TMAC-Urea, ChCl-Urea/DMSO and TMAC-Urea/ DMSO were shown in Fig. 2. It could be seen from the optimized geometries that the multiple active electronegative atoms and hydroxyl groups in the HBAs and HBDs structures conferred the ability to conduct hydrogen bonding interactions. And these atomic spacings were proven to be all within the acceptable criteria for hydrogen bond coordination (< 3.5 Å). Molecular electrostatic potential was a valid means for analyzing and predicting hydrogen bond interactions and was applied here to analyze the contributing effect of PAS solubility in DES. Further, the positive and negative average values of ESP could quantitatively provide information related to the solubility of the condensed phase that depended on non-covalent interactions (Murray & Politzer, 2011). As shown in the data of ESP analysis, the solubility of PAS presented a certain positive relationship with the corresponding overall average ESP value of each DES. ChCl-Urea had the largest overall average value of ESP (3.92 kcal/mol), and the plot of its surface area in each ESP range showed that the maximum area range (14.31%) was positive 32.67. In addition, it could be seen from Fig. S4 that the overall average value of ESP in ChCl-BDO with lower dissolving capacity was only 0.86 kcal/ mol, the surface area distribution in different ESP range was relatively uneven, with the largest area (25.04%) of just positive 7.00. Similarly, the overall lower average electrostatic potential of TMAC-Urea might influence the interactions with the hydroxyl groups of polysaccharides, resulting in lesser solubility. As shown in Fig. 3a, the highest occupied molecular orbitals (HOMO) electron cloud of ChCl-Urea was localized on chloridion, and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals (LUMO) electron cloud was mostly localized on the carbon and hydrogen atoms of the quaternary ammonium cation as well as the amino group of urea. These results could provide insights into forecasting the action sites between DES and PAS. It was well known that HOMO determined the region where elec-trons had the highest reaction energy, while LUMO established a region for filling with intruding electrons from other molecules during the bonding process (Dwamena & Raynie, 2020). Because of this, HOMO was related to the propensity to donate electrons, while LUMO was related to the propensity to accept electrons. Therefore, it was specu-lated that the LUMO region and HOMO region in ChCl-Urea might interact with the nucleophilic and potentiophilic sites in PAS, respec-tively. This finding was supported by the research of Zhang et al. that hydroxyl protons of cellulose could form strong hydrogen bonds with chloridions, and the intermolecular hydrogen bond networks of cellu-lose were broken during this process (Zhang et al., 2014). According to the above solubility phenomena together with the theoretical calculations and analysis, the studied DESs were full of hydrogen bond interactions and the multiple hydrogen bonding sites within the system provided their abilities to interact with PAS. Se-functionalization of PAS promoted by hydrogen bond modulation In this work, with the purpose of constructing a novel polysaccharide functionalization system, PAS was firstly Se-functionalized in the reaction system with DES as the solvent, while related control experiments were carried out under different solvent conditions at the same time. Table 2 presented selenium contents and yields of SePASs obtained under different conditions. Due to the weak solubility of PAS in DMSO (Fig. 2a), the selenium content of SePASDMSO (970.98 µg/g) obtained by the selenylation reaction conducted in DMSO were significantly lower. When DESs as reaction media, the selenium contents of corresponding SePASDES₁ and SePASDES₂ were elevated to 1535.60 and 2126.70 μg/g, respectively. It indicated that adequate solubilization of polysaccharide had a significant impact on determining the efficiency of subsequent functionalization. DES exhibited the dual properties of hydrogen bond providing and accepting abilities, and this characteristic brought about the superior solubilizing capacity of DES, which was supported by the above experimental and computational analysis. Therefore, it was probable that DES could break the hydrogen bond interactions between polysaccharide chains and expose more hydroxyl groups. In addition, the high viscosity of ChCl-Urea impeded the contact of substrates in the reaction system under sufficient solubilization condition, resulting in a compromised selenylation efficiency of SePASDES₁. The excellent dissolving capacity and lower viscosity of ChCl-EG might cause the seleno-groups to be more easily introduced into the polysaccharide chains, thus enhancing the efficiency of the selenylation reaction. Consequently, DES with multiple hydrogen bonding sites was capable of being a new type of selenylation medium. On the basis of the promising Se-functionalization effect of DES system, the co-solvent effect on the selenylation efficiency of PAS in DES/DMSO binary mixed solvents system was further explored. The selenium contents of SePAS₁ and SePAS₂ were 1947.46 and 4004.29 µg/g, which increased to a certain extent compared with the corresponding SePASDES₁ (1535.60 µg/g) and SePASDES₂ (2126.70 µg/g) obtained in pure DES systems. As shown in Fig. S6, the co-solvent strategy could reduce the viscosity of the reaction system and facilitate the contact between polysaccharides and H₂SeO₃ (Damstrup et al., 2006). Additionally, the binary mixed solvents system was shown in theoretical calculations and analysis to provide more hydrogen bonding sites in interaction with PAS (Section 3.3), allowing adequate exposure of PAS hydroxyl groups. The combination of the above two factors could lead to a better nucleophilic attack by hydroxyl groups, thus favoring the polysaccharide selenylation reaction. Similarly, Harifi-Mood et al. studied the reaction of 1-fluoro-2,4-dinitrobenzene with piperidine in DES/DMSO binary mixed solvents and found that the increase of DMSO was beneficial to elevate the reaction rate (Harifi-Mood & Sadrzadeh, 2018). This relationship was likely to be related to the fact that high polarity solvent was more conducive to the dissociation of anions and cations, which was beneficial to the destruction of hydrogen bonds within polysaccharide chains by chloridion and the subsequent major degradation of polysaccharide chains by acidic reaction envi- ronment. This also corresponded to the finding that both solubility and selenium content showed a correlation with polarity of DES. Likewise, the study of Liu et al. reported that the hydrogen bonds between chloride ions of DES and hydroxyl groups might weaken the strong hydrogen bond interactions in wood lignocellulose, thus breaking lignin- carbohydrate complexes linkages (Liu et al., 2017). Furthermore, the evolution of chain conformation in polysaccharide Se-functionalization mediated by DES/DMSO was investigated using MB and CR spectrophotometric method (Prentø, 2001). With increasing SePAS2 concentration, the gradual decrease at OD664nm of MB/SePAS2 absorption spectra and the progressive increase at OD554nm indicated that the positively charged MB interacted with the negatively charged SePAS2, which proved that seleno-groups were successfully introduced (Fig. 6c). Following this interactions, a long-range forces involving water and MB molecules appeared to bring the planar cationic molecules relatively close to each other and form metachromatic complexes, leading to selenium polysaccharide more inclined to rigid conformation (Michon et al., 2002). Meanwhile, it was observed that when SePAS2 concentration was 0.2 mg/mL, a large increase in NaOH destroyed the SePAS2/CR electrostatic interactions and disrupted the tendency for λmax of SePAS2/CR to be continuously red-shifting (Fig. 6d), which suggested that the rigid conformation of selenium polysaccharide (Tan et al., 2020). Similar results were reported by Liu et al. that the upward trend in λmax of polysaccharide/CR was influenced by the increasing NaOH concentration, confirming the extended conformation of polysaccharide (Liu et al., 2016). According to the above results, it was found that the M_W of SePAS was related to the polarity of DES, owing to the positive contribution of the high polarity DES to destruct the hydrogen bond networks of poly- saccharides, which further affected the degradation of polysaccharides by acid environment. Additionally, the DES/DMSO-mediated introduc- tion of seleno-group rendered the polysaccharide chains towards more rigid conformation. In summary, it might be possible to prospectively modulate the selenylation efficiency and polysaccharide M_W simulta- neously by constructing task-specific DESs with different HBAs/HBDs and solvent properties, which also provided new perspectives for the selection of solvent systems for polysaccharide derivatization reactions. ## 4. Conclusion The DES/DMSO binary solvents with more and stronger hydrogen bonding sites could coordinate the disruption and reconstruction of hydrogen bonds within polysaccharides, attaining superior solubilization ability than DES. The polysaccharide hydroxyl groups were fully exposed and activated in DES/DMSO-mediated novel Se-functionalization system owing to the disruption of the hydrogen bond networks, which facilitated selenylation efficiency and rendered acid-dependent M_w reduction. The obtained SePAS presented a tendency of rigid conformation due to the introduction of anion functional groups. In summary, this study supported further development of DESs with regulable solvent properties towards solubilization and functionalization high-value exploitation of heteropolysaccharide bioresources. This revealed that choline chloride-based DES/DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide) binary mixed solvents possessed more and stronger hydrogen bonding sites, facilitating the balance between disruption and reconstruction of hydrogen bonds within branched heteropolysaccharide from *Artemisia sphaerocephala* (PAS) and achieving efficient solubilization. Further, due to the full exposure and activation of polysaccharide hydroxyls, the efficiency of DES/ DMSO-mediated novel Se-functionalization was substantially enhanced compared to the conventional selenylation methods. The derivative exhibited conversion to lower molecular mass with rigid solution conformation based on co-solvent effect and predominant acidic environment influence. Introduction The ever increasing demands for resources in modern society and the promotion of environmental protection have led to a growing global concern for sustainable natural biological resource (Xu, Che, et al., 2019). In particular, polysaccharide resources of natural biological origin have been used in fuels, materials and pharmaceuticals (Mika et al., 2018). Limitations of structural properties make many natural polysaccharides biologically inactive, hence functionalization strategy becomes an effective way to develop polysaccharide resources (Li et al., 2016). However, owing to the complex structures and the presence of multiple hydrogen bond networks of polysaccharides, organic solvents that mediate polysaccharides functionalization in traditional reaction systems present poor abilities to dissolve polysaccharides and draw-backs such as wastewater contamination and biological toxicity (Farrán et al., 2015). The resulting non-homogeneous environment generally leads to reduced functionalization efficiencies of polysaccharides, which is not conducive to the exploitation of biological resources. Accordingly, the functionalized valorized development of natural resources requires new solvents and reaction media to achieve the mutual promotion and coordination between the efficient utilization of resources and ecolog- ical environmental protection. Green solvents are a class of environmentally friendly solvents that have been widely used in the development of biological resources in recent years, among which deep eutectic solvents (DESs) prepared by the hydrogen bond interactions between hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) and hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) are considered to possess great potential for macromolecular biotransformation (Hansen et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2012). The hydrogen bond providing/accepting ability of DESs can break hydrogen bonds between carbohydrates, while DESs exhibit high designability, low toxicity and low volatility (Chen & Mu, 2019). At the same time, the high viscosity and thermal decompo- sition exhibited by parts of DESs (González-Rivera et al., 2020; Rodri- guez Rodriguez et al., 2019) make the application of DESs to the processing of natural polysaccharides full of opportunities and chal- lenges. Moreover, the great dissolving performance of DES for poly- saccharide could be enhanced by building binary mixed solvents system to further reduce the viscosity, leading to lower experimental cost and * Corresponding author at: College of Life Science, Northwest Normal University, Anning Eastroad, Lanzhou, People's Republic of China. The dual solvent-solute/solvent interac- tion existing in the mixed solvents can further affect the reaction effi- ciency via solvent effects (Reichardt & Welton, 2011; Ruan et al., 2021). Hereby, much attention has been paid to investigating the interaction between co-solvents and DESs as well as the effect of modulating sol- vents on the functionalization of polysaccharide resources. Se-functionalization is an important approach to enhance the activity of natural polysaccharides and has been widely reported in recent years as a promising modification of natural polysaccharides (Li et al., 2019; Xu, Wu, et al., 2019). Our previous works achieved selenylation of natural heteropolysaccharide and revealed that in case of modified heteropolysaccharide, the introduction of anion functional groups and the tendency to a rigid solution conformation improved the bioactivities of anti-tumor (Liu et al., 2021) and immunomodulatory (Li et al., 2020). Moreover, compared with homopolysaccharide, heteropolysaccharide with diverse monosaccharide components and more branches resulting in critical problem of low substrate solubility, thereby leading to low subsequent conversion efficiency and harsh reaction environment. This is particularly evident in conventional polysaccharide selenylation systems, thus making the solvent as a key entry point for the construction of novel polysaccharide selenylation system (Guo et al., 2017). It has been demonstrated in many works that the hydrogen bond property of DES contributes to providing more hydrogen bonding sites, which is beneficial to break the hydrogen bond networks and promote the solubilization and subsequent functionalization reactions of polysaccharide (Cao et al., 2019). However, there is a relative paucity of empirical research specifically addressing the feasibility of DES for dissolving heteropolysaccharide and the effect of solvent composition regulation on dissolution capacity. For the highly solvent-dependent heteropolysaccharide processing, it is necessary to explore the prospect of DES as an effective solvent and reaction medium in the rather difficult selenylation reaction and expand the applicability of DES in the field of polysaccharide functionalization. Artemisia sphaerocephala is a kind of sand-fixing plant widely distributed in northwest China, and a branched heteropolysaccharide extracted from its seeds (PAS) showed a weight average molecular mass (M_w) of 6.96 × 10^4 g/mol (Wei et al., 2019). In this work, in order to break the bottleneck caused by heteropolysaccharide solubility limita- tion, a DES-mediated solvent system for PAS was proposed, and further quantum chemical calculations were used to investigate the interactions within mono and binary solvents systems to speculate the possible sol- ubility mechanism. Then, efficient DES-mediated Se-functionalizations of PAS and corresponding structural confirmations were carried out to explore the effect of this selenylation system on the conversion effi- ciency and heteropolysaccharide chain features. It is hoped that this research will contribute to a deeper understanding regarding the effect of DES on heteropolysaccharide solubilization and provide a reference for the investigation of DES performance modulation in biomolecular functionalization. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), choline chloride (ChCl), tetramethylammonium chloride (TMAC), ethylene glycol (EG), urea, glycerin (GLY), 1,4-butanediol (BDO), trifluoroacetic acid, hydroxylamine hydrochloride, pyridine, chloroform, Reichardt's dye (30) (RD), N,N-dimethyl-4-nitroaniline (DMNA), 4-nitroaniline (NA), ascorbic acid, potassium bromide (KBr), 2,3-diaminonaphthalene (DAN), ethylenediamine tetraacetate (EDTA-2Na), congo red (CR) and methylene blue (MB) were purchased from Jingchun Industry Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China. All chemicals used in present work were analytical reagents or better grades with no further purification. PAS was extracted and purified according to our previous study (Wei et al., 2019). In brief, crude PAS was extracted with distilled water at 80 °C for 18 h. All extraction solution was concentrated and then deproteinated using Sevag method to obtain purified PAS with M_W of 6.96 × 10^4 g/mol. The monosaccharide compositions of PAS were L-arabinose (Ara), D-xylose (Xyl), D-mannose (Man), D-glucose (Glc) and D-galactose (Gal) in molar ratio of 1: 4.33: 3.21: 4.63: 2.57. 2.2. The mixture in the sealed flask was stirred with a magnetic stirrer and heated at 80 °C until clear homogenous liquid was obtained. Heated for another 2 h, the mixture was placed in a glass vial and kept in a vacuum chamber at 50 °C to remove moisture from DES, then stored the glass vial in a desiccator to prevent moisture absorption. 2.3. Computational methods The initial structure optimization of DES was performed at HF/6-311G(d,p) level, and further reoptimization was obtained using the M06-2X exchange-correlation function in combination the 6-31++G(d,p) basis set based on the Gaussian 16 program package (Zhao & Truhlar, 2008). In order to reveal the non-covalent interactions in DES and DES/DMSO systems, the reduced density gradients (RDG) was calculated using Multiwfn program and the data were visualized by VMD and Gnuplot (Lu & Chen, 2012a). The electrostatic surface potential (ESP) of molecule was used to analyze hydrogen bond interactions, and the locations of the surface extrema and the statistical analysis of van der Waals (vdW) surface area in different ESP ranges were calculated referring to previous works (Lu & Chen, 2012b; Lu & Manzetti, 2014). For atoms in molecules (AIM) analysis, the electron density and Laplace amount of electron density at the bond critical point (BCP), namely ρ(BCP) and ∇²ρ(BCP), were commonly used to analyze the bond strength as well as covalent character (Lu & Chen, 2013). The reactivity of the solvent system was further analyzed by frontline molecular orbitals (FMO) theory in combination with Multiwfn program and VMD. ## 2.8. Characterization of hydrogen bond interactions in DESs As shown in Fig. 1a, the FT-IR spectra for HBAs, HBDs and the corresponding DESs were compared to prove hydrogen bond interactions. In DES$_{1-4}$, hydroxyl group stretching vibration was observed at 3333, 3347, 3354 and 3335 cm⁻¹ respectively, which showed blue shifts compared with ChCl (3255 cm⁻¹). Similarly, it could be noted that asymmetric stretching vibrations of the methyl in TMAC were at 2914 cm⁻¹, which shifted to 2969 cm⁻¹ for DES₅. On the other hand, the absorption peaks with strong intensity at 3357, 3374, and 3325 cm⁻¹ were attributed to hydroxyl group stretching vibration of the polyol HBDs (EG, GLY and BDO), which exhibited absorption peaks shifts when DESs were formed. These findings indicated the intermolecular hydrogen bond interactions between HBA and HBD. It was supported that the addition of HBD weakened the intermolecular hydrogen bonds of ChCl itself, which caused the blue shift effect of hydroxyl group stretching vibration of ChCl, demonstrating the formation of hydrogen bonds between HBA and HBD (Wang et al., 2019). The study reported by Hou et al. also demonstrated that the forming of strong hydrogen bonds resulted in hydroxyl group stretching vibration of HBD shifting from 3331 to 3218 cm⁻¹ (Hou et al., 2015). The hydrogen bond interactions between HBA and HBD were further investigated via ¹H NMR spectra of DES₁₋₈ (Fig. 1c). It was apparent that compared with HBA or HBD, the active hydrogen signal in corre-sponding DES upshifted for HBA and downshifted for HBD, which confirmed the existence of hydrogen bond interactions. As shown in Fig. S2, the chemical shift at 5.74 and 5.68 ppm corresponded to hy-droxyl group of ChCl and hydrogen atoms of urea, which shifted to 5.52 and 5.87 ppm in ChCl-Urea, respectively. This result might be explained by the fact that the formation of intermolecular hydrogen bonds be-tween ChCl and urea weakened the interactions between chloridion and hydroxyl group within ChCl, thus increasing the electron density of hydroxyl group and causing the chemical shift moving to high field. Meanwhile, hydroxyl group contributed to providing hydrogen bonding site resulting in the hydroxyl group signal of BDO shifting from 4.47 to 4.52 ppm in TMAC-BDO (Fig. S2). This result could be explained by the fact that the formation of hydrogen bonds caused the electron density of hydrogen atom in hydroxyl group reduction, which leading to the downshift of chemical shift (Hao et al., 2017). These findings matched the observation in previous studies that upshifting of the active hydrogen signal in HBA (tetraethylammonium hydroxide, from 0.91 to 0.74 ppm) and downshifting in HBD (GLY, from 3.681 to 3.798 ppm) (Sirviö & Heiskanen, 2020; Zaid et al., 2017). The system structures and optimized conformations of ChCl-Urea, TMAC-Urea, ChCl-Urea/DMSO and TMAC-Urea/ DMSO were shown in Fig. 2. It could be seen from the optimized geometries that the multiple active electronegative atoms and hydroxyl groups in the HBAs and HBDs structures conferred the ability to conduct hydrogen bonding interactions. And these atomic spacings were proven to be all within the acceptable criteria for hydrogen bond coordination (< 3.5 Å). Molecular electrostatic potential was a valid means for analyzing and predicting hydrogen bond interactions and was applied here to analyze the contributing effect of PAS solubility in DES. Further, the positive and negative average values of ESP could quantitatively provide information related to the solubility of the condensed phase that depended on non-covalent interactions (Murray & Politzer, 2011). As shown in the data of ESP analysis, the solubility of PAS presented a certain positive relationship with the corresponding overall average ESP value of each DES. ChCl-Urea had the largest overall average value of ESP (3.92 kcal/mol), and the plot of its surface area in each ESP range showed that the maximum area range (14.31%) was positive 32.67. In addition, it could be seen from Fig. S4 that the overall average value of ESP in ChCl-BDO with lower dissolving capacity was only 0.86 kcal/ mol, the surface area distribution in different ESP range was relatively uneven, with the largest area (25.04%) of just positive 7.00. Similarly, the overall lower average electrostatic potential of TMAC-Urea might influence the interactions with the hydroxyl groups of polysaccharides, resulting in lesser solubility. The possible dissolution mechanism of PAS in ChCl-Urea was pre-dicted by FMO analysis since the molecular orbitals were significant electronic parameters for describing the chemical reactivities of com-pounds. As shown in Fig. 3a, the highest occupied molecular orbitals (HOMO) electron cloud of ChCl-Urea was localized on chloridion, and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals (LUMO) electron cloud was mostly localized on the carbon and hydrogen atoms of the quaternary ammonium cation as well as the amino group of urea. These results could provide insights into forecasting the action sites between DES and PAS. It was well known that HOMO determined the region where elec-trons had the highest reaction energy, while LUMO established a region for filling with intruding electrons from other molecules during the bonding process (Dwamena & Raynie, 2020). Because of this, HOMO was related to the propensity to donate electrons, while LUMO was related to the propensity to accept electrons. Therefore, it was specu-lated that the LUMO region and HOMO region in ChCl-Urea might interact with the nucleophilic and potentiophilic sites in PAS, respec-tively. This finding was supported by the research of Zhang et al. that hydroxyl protons of cellulose could form strong hydrogen bonds with chloridions, and the intermolecular hydrogen bond networks of cellu-lose were broken during this process (Zhang et al., 2014). According to the above solubility phenomena together with the theoretical calculations and analysis, the studied DESs were full of hydrogen bond interactions and the multiple hydrogen bonding sites within the system provided their abilities to interact with PAS.
